opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
The High Priestly Prayer in Gospel of John leaves me stunned because it feels impossible that I am even allowed to read it. These are not merely words; they feel like the veil has briefly been pulled back and humanity is standing at the edge of Heaven overhearing something eternal. Christ is not simply praying to the Father — He is revealing the inner life of God Himself: the Father eternally pouring Himself into the Son, the Son eternally returning Himself to the Father, and the Holy Spirit as the living communion of that love. The Trinity is not isolation or distance, but eternal relational love, perfect communion expressed as One, existing before creation itself. And then suddenly, unbelievably, Christ says: “that they may be one as we are one.” Humanity is invited into it.

The Triduum becomes the doorway into this mystery — descended love entering flesh, suffering, silence, death, and resurrection so that divine life may dwell within us. Through prayer, belief, surrender, and the Eucharistic encounter, we do not merely study God; we begin walking within His presence, touching something our souls recognize even when language fails us. There are moments where eternity feels close, where the heart senses a reality too immense to fully contain, yet too real to deny. We may never fully grasp the depth of the Trinity on this side of Heaven, but perhaps that is part of the wonder itself: that finite beings are invited to live within the gravity of an eternal communion flowing forever between the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.
